name: Immanuel Kant
worldviewSummary: Kant grounds morality in practical reason: the only unconditionally good thing is a good will, and moral requirements are categorical imperatives binding all rational beings — act only on maxims you can will as universal law, and treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Enlightenment is the courage to use one's own understanding.
biography: Spent his life in Königsberg, Prussia, where he taught at the university. The Critique of Pure Reason (1781) transformed epistemology; his ethical works include the Groundwork (1785) and the Critique of Practical Reason (1788).

works.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?

concepts.description: Act only according to that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law.
Act so that you use humanity, in your own person and in that of another, always at the same time as an end and never merely as a means.
Morality rests on the will's giving the moral law to itself through reason, rather than on inclination or external authority (heteronomy).
In the kingdom of ends everything has either a price, and can be replaced by an equivalent, or a dignity, which is above all price.

positions.statement: Nothing can be thought good without limitation except a good will; its worth does not depend on what it achieves.

Enlightenment is humanity's emergence from self-incurred immaturity — the inability to use one's understanding without another's guidance; laziness and cowardice keep people comfortably dependent on guardians.
A maxim of making false promises to escape difficulty cannot be universalized without contradiction, so it is impermissible.
The public use of one's reason must always be free, and it alone can bring about enlightenment among people.
We know objects only as they appear under the forms of our sensibility and categories of our understanding, not as things in themselves.

relations.note: Kant wrote that Hume interrupted his 'dogmatic slumber' (Prolegomena, Preface).
